subject: Copywriting
title: L'Oréal: Because You're Worth It
description: A 60-second lesson on L'Oréal: Because You're Worth It.

hook.text: In 1973, a 23-year-old copywriter wrote 'Because I'm Worth It.' L'Oréal changed 'I'm' to 'You're.' A movement was born.

buildup.text: Ilon Specht wrote it as a response to women being told they didn't deserve premium products. It was a feminist act.

discovery.text: The slogan gives women permission to spend on themselves. It reframes a purchase as self-care, not vanity.

twist.text: In 2009, it evolved to 'Because We're Worth It'—adding community. Each pronoun shift reflected cultural change.

climax.text: The slogan has run for 50+ years across dozens of languages. Universal self-worth transcends culture.

punchline.text: A 23-year-old wrote a feminist slogan. It ran for 50 years.

quiz.question: What was the original pronoun in L'Oréal's slogan?

details.summary: L'Oréal's 'Because You're Worth It' was written in 1973 by 23-year-old copywriter Ilon Specht. It was revolutionary for speaking directly to women's self-worth at the height of the feminist movement. The slogan has evolved to 'Because We're Worth It,' reflecting shifting cultural values.
details.whyItMatters: This slogan proved that advertising could tap into social movements to create lasting brand loyalty. It gave women permission to spend on themselves — a radical idea in 1973.
takeaways: Ilon Specht wrote the slogan as a feminist statement at age 23
It justified premium pricing by appealing to self-worth
The evolution to 'We're Worth It' reflects inclusivity trends

faq.question: Why did L'Oréal change the slogan from 'You're' to 'We're'?
faq.answer: In 2009, L'Oréal shifted to 'Because We're Worth It' to create a sense of community and shared empowerment. The change also moved the brand voice from talking at consumers to standing alongside them.

faq.question: How did the slogan change cosmetics advertising?
faq.answer: Before 1973, beauty ads told women to look good for men. 'Because You're Worth It' flipped the script by saying women deserved luxury for themselves. This self-empowerment framing became the dominant approach in beauty marketing worldwide.
